store.0: I'm a fourth-year computer science major, and my hobbies are what keep me sane amidst the chaos of classes and projects. It's interesting how coding can be both intense and enjoyable at the same time. I find that my outside interests help me approach programming with a fresh perspective. Taking breaks is essential, as it prevents burnout and allows me to come back to coding with renewed energy.
store.1: Sailing is one of my favorite hobbies. It's unique among my friends, and I've been hooked since I was younger. My dad used to take me out on small sailboats near a marina near my hometown. Now, in college, I try to keep up with it during breaks. There's a local sailing club that offers boat rentals at a student-friendly rate. I'll sign up for a day, invite a friend if they're interested, and spend hours on the water. Sailing gives me a sense of freedom and a break from the chaos of deadlines, code bugs, and group project drama. It's a puzzle on a grand scale, which I think is why it appeals to my problem-solving side.
store.2: I'm really passionate about going to the gym regularly. In high school, I was the scrawny kid who spent most of his time hunched over a computer. Once I got to college, I realized I needed to balance out the screen time with some physical activity. I started with a basic lifting routine my freshman year, thanks to a friend who taught me proper form for squats and deadlifts, as well as how to program workouts. Now, I try to hit the gym around four times a week. It's not about becoming a bodybuilder; I just enjoy seeing incremental improvements. If I can lift a bit more weight this month than last, or if I have more energy in my daily life, I consider that a win. Additionally, it's a great stress-reliever after marathon coding sessions. The mental clarity I get after a good workout is incredible. It makes me more productive and helps me sleep better, especially on nights when I'm up late finishing an assignment.
store.3: Gaming is another hobby of mine that complements my interest in technology. I enjoy both PC and console games, but I spend more time on PC since it's my go-to platform as a CS major. Lately, I've been really into co-op survival games, where you gather resources, build shelters, and fend off creatures. This genre appeals to my problem-solving skills in a more relaxed environment compared to debugging codebases. Occasionally, I also engage in fast-paced shooters, especially when friends from class are online and we team up. Gaming is both a social activity and a mental challenge for me. While some might view it as a waste of time, I believe it can be strategic and collaborative, and it helps me stay connected. I've also dabbled in game development using Unity or Unreal Engine for fun. I'd like to explore this further if I have the time, as bridging the gap between playing games and creating them is fascinating.
store.4: Reading has been a lifelong passion of mine. My mom, who's a literature buff, used to introduce me to fantasy and sci-fi novels when I was a kid. I'd get lost in other worlds for hours. Even with a busy schedule now, I try to squeeze in some reading before bed or on weekends. Lately, I've been particularly interested in sci-fi novels that explore artificial intelligence. It's partly driven by my academic interests, as I enjoy imagining future technology and how it might blur the boundaries between humans and machines. My current favorite AI-themed sci-fi book is 'The Infinity Courts' by Akemi Dawn Bowman. Reading books like this helps me consider the ethical and social implications of the work I'll be doing after graduation. It's a way for me to explore philosophical questions related to my field in a more relaxed manner.
store.5: I've found that scheduling my hobbies helps me maintain a healthy balance. I plan out my week by checking the weather and seeing if I can fit in a gym session or a sailing trip to the local lake. If the weather isn't cooperating, I'll plan an indoor day with friends for co-op games or a workout in my apartment's fitness center. Reading is the easiest to fit in – I usually do 30 minutes before bed, which helps me unwind after a long day. It's all about finding time for the things that bring me joy and relaxation.
store.6: I enjoy combining my hobbies to create a diverse and engaging experience. For example, I've had a day where I spent the morning sailing at the lake, followed by lunch, and then spent the evening playing video games with friends. It was fascinating to notice how the experience on the water was similar to coordinating movement in an online co-op game. In both cases, everyone has a specific role – whether it's managing the sails or leading the in-game strategy. I love how each hobby requires teamwork, attention to detail, and problem-solving. It's great to see how they complement each other and provide a well-rounded experience.
store.7: It can be stressful, I won't deny it. My days are filled with lectures, labs, homework, research group meetings, and my part-time tutoring gig. However, when you're passionate about your hobbies, you'll find ways to make time for them, even if it's just in small increments. For example, I might not be able to read for hours, but I can read one chapter. I might not be able to sail every weekend, but once a month works. And with gaming, even 30 minutes is enough to squeeze in a quick match. It's all about finding ways to prioritize what brings you joy and relaxation.
store.8: I'm glad I can share my hobbies with you. They add a diverse range of experiences to my life, from the calming world of reading to the thrilling rush of sailing, from the discipline of weightlifting to the excitement of co-op games. It's wonderful to have these unique interests that showcase different sides of me. They make life more interesting and provide a break from the intensity of coding. I'm grateful for the opportunity to share my passions with you.
store.9: I've been involved in undergraduate research since the end of my sophomore year, and it's been one of the most eye-opening parts of my college experience. It's given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world, and it's pretty cool to be a part of that. As a freshman, I didn't see myself going down the research route. I was into coding projects and hackathons, but I didn't think of research as something that was 'my thing.' However, one of my professors, who taught an introductory data science class, noticed I had a knack for bridging technical coding with user experience. She told me about an opening for a research assistant in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific datasets. I was initially hesitant because research seemed intimidating. However, I decided to take the leap, and it turned out to be a great decision.
store.10: The lab I'm in is an interdisciplinary space where computer scientists partner with scientists from various backgrounds, such as astronomy, environmental science, and neuroscience, to make massive amounts of data more comprehensible. In classes, you often work with small data projects or tackle a 1GB dataset for a machine learning project. In our lab, we deal with datasets that are tens of terabytes in size. Visualizing such data so that domain experts(like astrophysicists) can quickly extract insights is a significant challenge. One of my main tasks is working on front-end prototypes that present slices of data in dynamic, interactive dashboards. This involves using advanced JavaScript frameworks, D3.js for custom visualizations, and specialized libraries for volumetric rendering if we're dealing with 3D data.
store.11: The first research project I really got into was about visualizing oceanic temperature changes over time for a climate study group. They had these daily temperature readings from buoys all around the Pacific. The raw data was enormous, with tons of files scattered across different servers, each representing a single day's worth of readings at tiny intervals. Our job was to aggregate and present them in a coherent way that could show patterns over months or even years. I dove in headfirst: writing scripts to clean and unify the data, building a pipeline that could handle near real-time updates, and then designing interfaces that let researchers zoom into a particular region or timeframe. Eventually, I co-authored my first paper on this system. I won't lie, I freaked out a bit when I saw my name in an official publication – it felt surreal, and it's probably one of my proudest moments in college.
store.12: These days, my research has pivoted to something slightly different but still under the umbrella of data visualization: immersive analytics platforms. We're exploring how VR or AR technologies might help scientists get an even more intuitive feel for complex data. Looking at raw numerical data in a spreadsheet is one thing, and 2D visuals like graphs are another step up. However, being able to walk around a 3D representation of data in a virtual environment, touch it, rotate it, and highlight subsets might be a game-changer for some fields. It's definitely a leap from just coding up websites. There's a lot of experimentation, plugging in VR headsets, integrating with engines like Unity or Unreal, and figuring out how to efficiently stream data into a 3D environment. It's all super cutting-edge, but that's what makes it fun. Every day, you're forging your own path because there isn't a huge, established best-practice library for VR data visualization yet.
store.13: Now, let me talk about the nitty-gritty of research life. A lot of people imagine it as me sitting in a quiet corner coding away at some mysterious project, but actually, it's a lot of reading. Academic papers never end. If I'm trying to solve a bug with how to render certain volumetric data in VR, there's a good chance someone has tried something similar, wrote about it in a conference proceeding or workshop, and I need to comb through it. It can get overwhelming, but over time, you learn how to skim effectively – looking at the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to see if a paper is relevant before diving into all the details. Occasionally, when I discover something interesting, I'll share it with the rest of the lab, and we'll discuss how we can incorporate that technique into our own workflow.
store.14: I also get to interact with a bunch of graduate students – both master's and PhDs. It can be intimidating at first because they're so deeply immersed in their niche fields, but it's also inspiring. There's this one PhD student in our lab who's been developing a machine learning algorithm to do on-the-fly compression of large datasets. He's trying to integrate it with our VR platform. The idea is that if you're looking at a huge climate dataset, you don't need to have every single point fully loaded at once in VR – a compressed representation might be enough until you zoom in. It's wild, but super practical for real-time performance. Working alongside him means I get to see how advanced theoretical concepts actually get applied. Some of our best brainstorming sessions happen spontaneously – like in the lab break room, sipping coffee and hashing out how we can offload some processing to the GPU.
store.15: We've also done a few poster presentations at smaller symposiums around campus, which was a great experience. You have to boil down complex research into easy-to-digest visuals and talking points. The first time I presented, I was sweating bullets. The idea of random professors or industry folks walking by and asking tough questions really freaked me out. But it turned out to be more like a friendly dialogue. People are genuinely interested in what you're doing. There were even a few folks from local startups who showed up, and they had some interesting perspectives on how VR for data visualization could benefit commercial industries – like marketing analytics or even architecture. It opened my eyes to how research can transition from academia to real-world applications.
store.16: As for publications, I've been lucky enough to be a co-author on two workshop papers and I'm currently working on a larger conference submission. The bigger conference is the IEEE Visualization Conference(commonly known as IEEE VIS), which is a pretty big deal in our area. We're focusing on a user study that compares traditional 2D dashboards with an interactive VR environment. Our hypothesis is that VR immersion helps researchers spot anomalies or trends faster than they would with just a plain old 2D chart. We ran a small set of user trials – like 15 participants – recorded their times, asked them to fill out a UX questionnaire, and all that jazz. Now we're crunching the data to see if there's a statistically significant difference. Writing the paper is a group effort: I'm handling the sections on system architecture and prototype design, someone else is writing about the user study methodology, and our PI(principal investigator) is weaving it all into a cohesive narrative. It's definitely a balancing act, especially since I have my senior coursework and a capstone project to manage.
store.17: Sometimes I get asked if I plan on going to grad school myself. Right now, I'm leaning towards working in the industry for a couple of years – hopefully at a tech company that values R&D or advanced solution building – before deciding if I want to pursue a master's or PhD. The idea of contributing to cutting-edge knowledge is really tempting, especially in areas like data visualization or machine learning. However, I also want to see how these concepts get applied in real product development. One of my mentors in the lab said that sometimes stepping into industry can give you a better perspective on what problems are truly relevant, so that if you do come back for a PhD, you'll have a more practical approach.
store.18: Oh, and I'd be lying if I said it's all been sunshine and rainbows. Research can be frustrating. You'll spend weeks on an approach that doesn't pan out, or you'll discover your entire idea has already been done—and improved upon—by a group in Europe or somewhere else. That part can feel like a punch in the gut. But the key is to adapt. We'll read that existing paper, incorporate their findings, either think of a new angle or a new application, and push the boundary. That's the essence of research. You're never truly starting from scratch; you're building on this giant foundation of what others have done. The sense of collaboration – both within our lab and among the global research community – is something I find really special.
store.19: One story that really stands out: a few months ago, one of our massive servers crashed. We had vital data stored there – some of which wasn't fully backed up(I know, rookie mistake, but we learned from it). I remember the scramble that night: a frantic email chain, Zoom calls with the lab manager, everyone trying to see if we could recover the data. We did manage to restore most of it, but that crisis hammered home the importance of data backups. After that fiasco, we set up a better backup system, plus some checks to ensure we never again rely on a single point of failure. It was stressful, but also kind of a bonding experience for the whole lab.
store.20: Another big plus is that research connects me with professors on a more personal level than just being a face in the lecture hall. My PI is super approachable; if I have a question about the direction of my career or even something I'm struggling with in class, I know I can pop into her office and chat. She's been recommending me for different scholarships, events, and networking opportunities. I got to attend a virtual workshop on immersive analytics that was filled with academic experts from all around the world. Getting to see them debate technical details, propose new frameworks, and even gently tease each other over rival theories was fascinating. It was like I was witnessing the frontier of CS knowledge in real time.
store.21: So yeah, that's basically my journey in the research world so far. It's a lot of work, often more chaotic than you'd expect, but also super rewarding. I love the feeling that what I do in the lab might end up shaping the way scientists understand their data five or ten years down the line. Maybe one day the VR and immersive stuff we're trying to pioneer will become standard tools, and I'll be able to look back and say, 'Hey, I was part of that from the beginning.' It's that sense of contributing to something bigger that really keeps me motivated. Whether or not I go to grad school soon, I know this experience has changed how I think about computer science, about innovation, and even about teamwork. I couldn't imagine my undergrad years without it – it's definitely enriched my whole perspective on what it means to be a computer scientist.
store.22: I've been a fourth-year Computer Science student here for a while now, and I've seen how the campus culture has evolved over the years. There are so many different communities that make this place feel like a second home. There are ways to get involved beyond just coding all day.
store.23: I've been exploring software engineering roles that align with my passions in data visualization, VR/AR technologies, and data-driven product development. Through my research experience, I've developed a love for making complex datasets interactive and approachable. I'm drawn to companies that push boundaries in data analytics or immersive technologies, such as Unity, Unreal, or smaller startups specializing in VR solutions for healthcare or engineering. My lab mentor advised me to follow the domain that excites me, not just the biggest names. I'm considering both the well-known tech giants like Google, Amazon, and Facebook, as well as smaller companies where I can make a bigger impact earlier on.
store.24: I'm currently in the midst of campus recruiting, with career fairs that can be both exhilarating and stressful. I've already submitted a number of applications, mostly for software engineering or data engineering intern-to-full-time conversion roles. I did an internship last summer at a tech startup specializing in data analytics software for logistics companies. It was a valuable experience as I got to see how a real development team operates, including sprint planning, code reviews, and feature rollouts to paying clients. My tasks ranged from building small UI components for their analytics dashboard to writing data pipelines that process shipping events in near real-time. By the end of that internship, I felt more confident in my skills, which I believe will help me stand out during interviews.
store.25: I'm torn between the idea of continuing my research in immersive analytics or human-computer interaction for large datasets. Advanced degrees can open doors to specialized R&D roles in industry labs or academia. Writing workshop papers and working on a conference submission has shown me that I enjoy exploring a single topic in-depth and pushing the boundaries. However, there's a practical consideration: I'd like to apply what I've learned in a commercial setting for a while before committing to a PhD or even a master's program. Some peers suggest doing a part-time master's while working, while others advise going all-in if I decide to pursue it. It's a tough decision to make.
store.26: My involvement in various campus clubs and projects has significantly shaped my vision for the future. Participating in group-driven assignments, such as my current capstone project analyzing social media sentiment for emergency responses, has taught me the value of teamwork and problem-solving in high-pressure situations. It's not just about coding for me; it's about collaborating with others, brainstorming solutions, creating prototypes, learning from failures, and iterating until they work. I want a role that encourages cross-functional collaboration with designers, data scientists, product managers, or domain experts from non-tech fields. The interdisciplinary environment I've enjoyed in my research lab is something I'd like to continue in my professional life.
store.27: Financial considerations are also important. I have some student loans, and I'm conscious about wanting a stable income soon after graduation. I need to think about health insurance, paying rent, and saving up. A full-time engineering position typically comes with a decent salary, which would help me pay off my debt faster. If I went straight into grad school, funding can be complicated, with some programs offering stipends and others not. Master's programs often require tuition payments, and scholarships can be competitive. Having a job in industry could serve a dual purpose: alleviating financial strain and providing career momentum, allowing me to decide if I truly want to go back to school.
store.28: The timeline is also important. Many companies do their hiring in waves, especially for new grads. I need to stay on top of deadlines and continue with interview prep, which can be grueling, especially with algorithmic challenges, system design scenarios, and domain-specific tests for specialized roles. I set aside a couple of hours each week to practice problems, brush up on coding patterns, and revisit data structures and algorithms. While I don't enjoy the interview grind, I understand its purpose. Fortunately, the advanced courses I'm taking, such as Advanced Algorithms and Distributed Systems, are boosting my confidence for those technical screens. I've become more comfortable discussing topics like concurrency, big-O notation, and analyzing architecture design trade-offs.
store.29: A few companies have already reached out for initial chats, which is surreal, especially when you're still trying to keep up with assignments. I'm trying not to get too carried away, knowing that a recruiter message is just the beginning of the hiring process. However, I'm optimistic. I'm also exploring smaller companies or startups in my city or nearby tech hubs, as they often offer more hands-on roles where you can learn from day one. The idea of joining a brand-new VR startup, having a stake in its success, and building a product from scratch is incredibly appealing, especially to my entrepreneurial side.
store.30: I've entertained the idea of launching my own venture, but I'm not planning to do it right after graduation. I think it's too risky. However, after gaining some industry experience, I might consider it. I have a couple of ideas for VR-based training simulators or interactive data analytics platforms. If I team up with talented friends from my advanced classes or the research lab, we could potentially spin up a small venture. I'm aware of the challenges of maintaining a startup, especially without a guaranteed paycheck. My parents have been supportive, but they also remind me to stay grounded and consider living expenses. They emphasize financial independence as a crucial aspect of life after college.
store.31: Family is another factor to consider. My parents live in a different state, so I need to think about how far I'm willing to move. Tech hubs like Silicon Valley, Seattle, Austin, and even Midwest cities are attractive options. While I'm not opposed to relocating, I also know that being far from family can make it difficult to visit. Some of my upperclassmen friends who graduated last year say that remote or hybrid roles have changed the game, allowing them to live near family or in their preferred locations while still working for a big name or innovative startup. It's a great time to be entering the tech workforce, with many options available, but it can be overwhelming to navigate them all.
store.32: I know that I want to continue growing my skills and avoid complacency. Even if I land a role that's not perfect, as long as I'm learning new frameworks, approaches to product development, or management skills, I'll consider it a success. My biggest fear is stagnation, especially in a field that evolves rapidly. Wherever I go, I plan to stay curious, push my boundaries, and specialize in immersive tech for data. That's my goal. Next steps include finishing senior year strong, continuing to interview, and seeing which offers come my way. I aim to make a decision by late spring. I'm excited about the potential paths ahead and confident that I'll figure it out, no matter what.
